name: Nora Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. What's a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Ashcombe Farm, which is my husband Dan's family farm, about two hundred and fifty acres: beef cattle, a flock of sheep, wheat and potatoes, and a little shop at the gate. I feed the cattle in the morning, check the sheep, and from ten I run the shop, eggs, potatoes, our own beef in the freezer. Dan does the crops, and his dad, Ron, still owns the place and still thinks he runs it. Four years ago I was a bank cashier, so I'm still very much learning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The bank closed our branch in Ashcombe, everyone went online, and I was out after seventeen years. Dan said come and work with us, so I did. Ron pays me a proper wage, more than most farm hands round here get, and I had the redundancy money too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the shop most, it's the bank counter all over again, people telling me their news. The cattle I'm still nervous with, I let Dan do the bull. What wears me down is Ron's paperwork and the phone apps Dan keeps showing me, I won't use them, I write it in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it's always the same, the salesmen promise the moon. Computers closed my bank branch in Ashcombe, so I'll believe AI is hype when the bank reopens. I'd say that at the shop counter and people would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, it means nothing changes for us, and that suits me. We've got the farm, Dan, the savings, the kids are settled at school. The only worry I have is the usual one, who gets the farm when Ron goes, and whether Dan's sister wants her share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep doing the cattle mornings and the shop, keep writing it all in the diary. I'd maybe ask Dan to let me do the sheep scanning course in the winter, because I'm still slow with the flock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Like nothing's coming through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the question of who inherits.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ron's seventy-two and won't talk about it. Dan's sister, Clare, lives in the city and would want her half in money, which could mean selling land. It's not AI, but it's the thing that keeps me up when anything does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you miss the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I miss the people and the coffee on Fridays. I don't miss the targets. Here nobody tells me to sell a credit card to a pensioner.

say: The **salesmen promised** the moon, as always.
Computers closed **my bank branch**, so I'll believe AI is hype when it reopens.
think: Nothing changes for the family, and the **farm and savings** feel secure.
My real worry is **who inherits** Ashcombe when Ron goes.
do: **Carry on** with cattle mornings and the farm shop.
**Keep** records in the paper diary, not apps.
**Ask** Dan about a sheep scanning course this winter.
feel: **Comfortable**, like nothing is coming through the door.
S0.quote: Computers closed my bank branch in Ashcombe, so I'll believe AI is hype when the bank reopens.
fieldNote: She has already **lost a job** to computers, which colours everything.
Her only real pressure is **farm succession**, not technology.
Prefers the **paper diary** over Dan's apps, a firm habit.

steps.text: Keep running the farm shop and morning cattle feed
Ask Dan about a sheep scanning course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's safer than banking was, because you can't feed a cow over the internet. But I'd also say watch the paperwork, the subsidy forms and the ordering, those go to the computer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father-in-law Ron reads the robot feeder brochure at the kitchen table like it's a holiday magazine. If robots spread, even slowly, the cattle feeding is the first thing that goes, and that's my job. They wouldn't sack me, I'm family, but what would I do all morning?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, honestly, I wouldn't rush anything. I'd put a bit more aside each month in case my wage shrinks. And I'd keep the shop going, maybe longer hours in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've seen this film before at the bank, it starts with a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the bank, before the branch closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First they put in the machines in the wall, then the online app, then they cut our hours. Then a letter. It took about three years from the first machine to the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ron how you feel about the robot feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not directly. I'd tell Dan, and Dan would tell Ron in his own way. That's how things get said in this family.

say: Farming's **safer than banking**, because you can't feed a cow online.
The **subsidy forms** and ordering go to computers first.
think: Ron is already reading a **robot feeder** brochure.
Feeding is **her job**; she'd keep a wage but lose her mornings.
do: **Set aside** a bit more each month in case her wage shrinks.
**Open** the farm shop longer in summer.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the bank closure also started with a brochure.
S1.quote: My father-in-law Ron reads the robot feeder brochure at the kitchen table like it's a holiday magazine.
fieldNote: Pattern-matches to the **bank closure**: brochure, machines, letter.
Family farm means she won't be sacked but may **lose her role**.
Speaks to Ron **through Dan**, a family dynamic that limits her say.

steps.text: Hold off any change until the robot feeder decision is made
Save an extra amount each month from her wage
Open the farm shop longer on summer evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the bank all over again, only bigger, and nobody listened last time either. I'd tell the women at the shop to keep their savings safe. I wouldn't go online about it, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking stuff in 2028 hits Ron's forms and Dan's crop planning, not me. Then 2031, the robots do the feeding, the sheep checking, maybe even the potato grading. I'm forty-three now, I'd be forty-eight, and I'd be the family member with no job on the family farm. My wage could shrink to nothing, and it's my own money, I've always had my own money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit Dan and Ron down and get the farm handover sorted, with my name on something, because that's my real safety. I'd put most of my wage into savings from now. And I'd grow the shop, because a robot can feed cattle, but it can't stand behind a farm shop counter and remember that Mrs Hale's (a regular customer's) husband just died.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicking, we'd eat, but worried for my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having your own money mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum never had her own account, my dad gave her housekeeping. I swore I'd always earn. Being kept by the farm would sit badly with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would three years' warning change your view of the apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd learn the till for the shop if I had to, but I'm not talking to a robot about cattle. The shop is people, that's where I'd put my effort.

say: It's the **bank all over again**, only bigger.
Keep your **savings safe**, she'd tell the women at the shop.
think: By 2031 robots could do **feeding and sheep checks**, her whole job.
She'd be the family member with **no job**, losing her own wage.
do: **Settle** the farm handover with Dan and Ron, with her name included.
**Save** most of her wage from now.
**Grow** the farm shop as her people-based role.
feel: **Worried** for her place, though not panicking about food.
S2.quote: A robot can feed cattle, but it can't stand behind a farm shop counter and remember that Mrs Hale's (a regular customer's) husband just died.
fieldNote: Her own **independent income** matters deeply, rooted in her mother's story.
Uses the **three years** to secure ownership rather than retrain.
Still refuses AI; puts her effort into **people work** at the shop.

steps.text: Settle the Ashcombe handover with Dan and Ron, with her name on it
Save most of her monthly wage from now
Grow the farm shop with a beef box for regulars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic, but don't pretend either. Same as I'd tell a customer about their savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can watch the neighbours buy the robots first and learn from their mistakes. The Hollands next door always buy the new thing, they had the first quad bike round here. By 2034 I'd know whether it works and whether I need to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait, and watch the Hollands. In the meantime I'd build the shop slowly, maybe add a coffee machine and a bench. And I'd still want the handover sorted, but without the rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Some worry, but I can see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the Hollands' robots work brilliantly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Ron will want one by the next week, and Dan will agree. I'd have the shop by then. I'd make my peace with it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ellie and Sam about their futures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie wants to be a vet, and I'd say go for it, animals need people. Sam's ten and only cares about football, so that can wait.

say: There's **time**, so don't panic, but don't pretend either.
It's the same advice she'd give a **bank customer** about savings.
think: She can watch the **Holland family** buy robots first and learn.
By 2034 she'd know whether she **needs to change**.
do: **Watch** the Hollands' robots before deciding anything.
**Add** a coffee machine and bench to the farm shop.
**Keep** the handover talk going without rushing.
feel: **Steadier**, with worry she can see coming.
S3.quote: Five years means I can watch the neighbours buy the robots first and learn from their mistakes.
fieldNote: Classic **resistant** strategy: let early adopters go first.
The shop is her **steady anchor** across scenarios.
Daughter's **vet plans** reassure her: animals still need people.

steps.text: Watch how the Hollands' robots work before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time in farming, look how much changed in the last ten. Nobody can plan that far out properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years from now I'll be fifty-three, and I'd rather be selling eggs to people than watching a screen. Robots in 2039 is somebody else's farm, Dan will probably have handed over to Ellie or nobody by then. I'm not losing sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep the shop, keep the cattle mornings while I have them. I'd only change things when the robots were really here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's too far away to bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about 2036 that bothers you, even far off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids' jobs, maybe. Ellie would be a newly qualified vet in 2036, I'd want to know if AI is doing the vets' thinking work by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start saving more anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We save already. I wouldn't change it for something ten years away.

Look how much changed in the **last ten years**.

Robots in 2039 feel like **someone else's farm**.
do: **Carry on** with the shop and cattle mornings.
feel: **Calm**; it's too far away to bother her.
S4.quote: Ten years from now I'll be fifty-three, and I'd rather be selling eggs to people than watching a screen.
fieldNote: Long horizons make her **disengage** rather than plan.

steps.text: Keep running the farm shop and morning cattle feed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years from robots to my job going is what happened at the bank. What would help is the farm handover being done properly, with my name in it, so I've got something that's mine whatever the machines do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people like me have been through this already. I have, at the bank. Twice in one life is too many times to be told a machine does your job better.

headlineQuote: Twice in one life is too many times to be told a machine does your job better.
portrait: Former **bank cashier** whose branch closed; now four years on her husband's family farm.
Runs the **farm shop** and morning cattle feeding, and won't use apps.
Money is secure, but she values her **own wage** deeply.
Calm in the plateau, **anxious** at AGI by 2028, when robots could leave her no farm role.
Her plan is ownership: getting her **name on the handover**, and growing the shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which repeats the bank: three years from machines to losing her role.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **farm handover** with her name in it, so something is hers.
